name: Contour Lines
basis: isolines of brightness by marching squares (how)
note: A cartographic convention, not a making process.

lumenary.blurb: Your picture read as a landscape, with brightness for height. Every line joins points of equal height, as on a survey map.

why: A contour line joins points of the same height, and on a map where lines crowd together the ground is steep. Reading your picture’s brightness as height turns it into a landscape and lets the same map language describe it: tight lines at sharp edges, wide gaps in the smooth parts, a heavier line at regular steps to help the eye count.
how: Smooth the lightness by the chosen radius and treat it as a height F(x, y).
For each level k/n, find the line F = k/n with marching squares on cells about 1.5 px wide.
Find where the line crosses each cell side by interpolation: t = (level − F_a)/(F_b − F_a).
Chain the pieces into long polylines and draw them as smooth curves.
Draw every fifth line heavier as an index contour, and tint the bands between.
history: Edmond Halley published a map of lines of equal magnetic variation in 1701, among the first uses of lines of equal value. In the 1770s, during the experiment on the Scottish mountain Schiehallion, Charles Hutton used contour lines to calculate the mountain’s volume. Contours became the standard way to show relief on topographic maps in the nineteenth century.
uses: Weather charts with isobars and isotherms
terms: A line joining points of equal height.
A heavier line drawn at regular steps for easy reading.
Any line of equal value, such as pressure or temperature.
paragraphs: A contour line joins the points of a landscape that have the same height. The program reads the picture’s lightness as height, F(x, y), after smoothing it by the slider’s radius, and draws the lines F = k/n for k = 1, …, n − 1, where n is the number of heights. To find a line it uses marching squares: the picture is covered by little cells (about 1.5 px wide), and the cells whose corners are partly above and partly below the level are crossed by the line. Its position on a side comes from linear interpolation, t = (level − F_a)/(F_b − F_a). The pieces are chained into long polylines and drawn as smooth quadratic curves. Where the picture changes quickly the lines crowd together, since their spacing is about 1/(n |∇F|), as on a map where the hill is steep.

Mapmakers draw every fifth or so line heavier (an index contour) and tint the bands between. Both are here: the heavier line is 1.9 times as thick, set by the heavier-line-every slider. The tint is a hypsometric ramp from green through ochre and brown to snow-white, evaluated at the middle of each band, or the picture’s own colours flattened to the band by scaling each colour by (0.55 + 0.6 b)/(0.55 + 0.6 F). Lines can be ink, brown like old maps, or the colour of the picture darkened.

equations.tex: C_k=\Big\{\mathbf x:\ F(\mathbf x)=\tfrac{k}{n}\Big\},\qquad \Delta s\approx\frac{1}{n\,\lVert\nabla F\rVert}
equations.note: The contour of height k/n and the spacing between neighbouring lines.
Where a contour crosses a cell side between corner values F_a and F_b, for the level λ (marching squares).
The band value that picks the tint between two lines.

presets.text: Many levels with the picture tinting each band look like a survey map.
Heavy smoothing turns the picture into gentle hills.
No fill and ink lines look like a pen drawing.
